subject: Problem with mixture model and prior

messages.author: e1c430550f86b1f6
messages.subject: Problem with mixture model and prior
parts:
Hi all,

I tried to create 2 different mixtures within a STAN program - where one was given a prior and the other was not.

However, under certain circumstances, it seems that giving a prior to one of the mixture would affect other variables be fitted

Attached files as follow:
data.r: list supplied to rstan

base.stan - in this version, I use STAN to create 2 identical mixture of normal.
prior.stan  - in this version, i apply a normal to one of the 2 mixtures.
alt.stan    - in this version, i do non-parameter (new_forecast) as the means of the mixture components

r.out - rstan results/output

My question is:
While the normal prior is applied to live_forecast_j, the values of fund_forecast seems to be affected.

From base.stan, we have the values of fund_forecast as:
                  mean se_mean   sd  2.5%   25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
fund_forecast[1] -0.07    0.01 0.23 -0.50 -0.17 -0.07  0.05  0.33   828    1
fund_forecast[2] -0.03    0.00 0.20 -0.43 -0.14 -0.03  0.08  0.39  2083    1

From prior.stan, we have quite different results
                  mean se_mean   sd  2.5%   25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
fund_forecast[1] -0.02    0.00 0.20 -0.41 -0.14 -0.03  0.09  0.37  2079    1
fund_forecast[2]  0.01    0.00 0.19 -0.34 -0.09  0.01  0.11  0.40  1794    1

But, alt.stan give similar results to base.stan
                  mean se_mean   sd  2.5%   25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
fund_forecast[1] -0.06    0.00 0.20 -0.46 -0.17 -0.06  0.05  0.34  3205    1
fund_forecast[2] -0.02    0.00 0.20 -0.42 -0.14 -0.03  0.09  0.41  2654    1

My question is - why should fund_forecast be affected by assigning a prior to one of the mixtures?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problem with mixture model and prior
parts:
Unless variables are marginally independent given data,
putting a prior on one will affect the other. And all
your variables appear related.

That is, a mixture model isn't equivalent to fitting all the
data with component one, fitting all the data with component two,
then mixing them. Everything's fit jointly.

You can see how this works in a simple mixture of two normal
cases. Compare the effect of the prior on one of the two
means (assume equal variance to keep it really simple).

- Bob
